During the height of the US-China trade war under Trump, tariffs were being adjusted almost weekly, and companies like Logitech quickly raised prices on their US products significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled these tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. However, no company has yet passed those refunds on to consumers, and a class action lawsuit is currently underway to try to correct this situation...

Trump's Tariff Storm

Last year, Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China, seemingly fantasizing that imposing heavy tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the US.

Of course, that never happened. The US lacks the infrastructure, expertise, and cheap labour needed to manufacture consumer electronics at the scale major brands require.

Trump kept insisting that China would pay the tariffs, but the reality is that these costs were paid by US brands importing finished goods, and the added expense was ultimately passed on to consumers through higher prices. At the peak of the storm, tariff rates briefly soared as high as 145%.

Take Logitech for example — the company raised prices on roughly half its products by up to 25%.

Consumers Deserve a Refund

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that companies must be refunded the amounts they paid. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher product prices, and none of the affected companies have indicated they will refund consumers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class action lawsuit against Logitech on this basis, seeking refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's Take

The principle behind the case is indisputable. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and are now receiving refunds from the government. Morally, they should refund the corresponding portion to consumers who bought products during that period.

However, implementing this is extremely challenging. Logitech would need to identify every transaction across its vast network of third-party retailers, track the prices consumers paid, and calculate what proportion of that was tariff cost.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it would set a very interesting precedent — though it must be pointed out that in class action lawsuits, the ones who truly profit are usually the lawyers, while consumers typically receive very little in actual compensation.
